bib.title: Larger language models do in-context learning differently

question: How much does in-context learning rely on semantic priors from pretraining versus on input-label mappings shown in the exemplars, and how does that change with model scale and instruction tuning?
hypothesis: Larger models may be able to override semantic priors and learn input-label mappings in context, even though they presumably hold stronger priors.
contributions: Flipped-label ICL shows overriding semantic priors is an emergent ability of scale.
SUL-ICL (semantically-unrelated labels) shows learning input-label mappings without semantic priors also emerges with scale, including linear classification.
Instruction tuning improves input-label mapping learning but strengthens semantic priors more.

method.summary: Prompts frozen pretrained and instruction-tuned LMs with few-shot classification exemplars under three label conditions: natural, flipped (a proportion of exemplar labels swapped) and semantically-unrelated (Foo/Bar). Accuracy is measured on unmodified evaluation labels as scale, exemplar count and instruction tuning vary.
method.task: few-shot in-context text classification (seven tasks) plus synthetic N-dimensional linear classification

datasets.name: SST-2
datasets.size: 100 randomly sampled evaluation examples per dataset (default)
datasets.split: exemplars from training set, evaluation from validation set; random 80/20 split where none exists

datasets.name: SUBJ
datasets.size: 100 randomly sampled evaluation examples per dataset (default)
datasets.split: exemplars from training set, evaluation from validation set; random 80/20 split where none exists

datasets.name: TREC
datasets.size: 100 randomly sampled evaluation examples per dataset (default)
datasets.split: exemplars from training set, evaluation from validation set; random 80/20 split where none exists
datasets.preprocessing: six coarse labels; excluded from flipped-label experiment (six classes); natural labels Human Being, Entity, Description and Abstract Concept, Abbreviation, Location, Numeric Value

datasets.name: QQP
datasets.size: 100 randomly sampled evaluation examples per dataset (default)
datasets.split: exemplars from training set, evaluation from validation set; random 80/20 split where none exists
datasets.preprocessing: natural labels 'Duplicate' / 'Not a duplicate'; the two questions of a pair are on consecutive lines in one Input

datasets.name: RTE
datasets.size: 100 randomly sampled evaluation examples per dataset (default)
datasets.split: exemplars from training set, evaluation from validation set; random 80/20 split where none exists
datasets.preprocessing: excluded for PaLM in Fig 16/17 because k=16 prompts exceed context length; natural labels 'Entails' / 'Does not entail'; premise and hypothesis on consecutive lines in one Input

datasets.name: FP
datasets.size: 100 randomly sampled evaluation examples per dataset (default)
datasets.split: exemplars from training set, evaluation from validation set; random 80/20 split where none exists
datasets.preprocessing: sentences_allagree subset; natural labels 'Positive' / 'Negative' (no neutral class, sentences_allagree subset)

datasets.name: ETHOS
datasets.size: 100 randomly sampled evaluation examples per dataset (default)
datasets.split: exemplars from training set, evaluation from validation set; random 80/20 split where none exists
datasets.preprocessing: binary subset; natural labels 'Hate Speech' / 'Not Hate Speech'

datasets.name: Synthetic N-dimensional linear classification
datasets.source: generated by Algorithm 1, integer coordinates 1 to 1000
datasets.preprocessing: 16-dimensional example prompt in App D.8: 'Input: <16 comma-separated integers>', labels Foo (negative) / Bar (positive), SUL-ICL only

datasets.name: Rotten Tomatoes (RT)
datasets.source: Pang & Lee 2005; OOD test with SST-2 (App B.6)

inference.samples: one run; a different random set of exemplars per inference example; 100 evaluation examples per dataset; no seeds or variance reported
inference.prompting: k = 16 exemplars per class by default (2, 4, 8, 16 in the exemplar sweeps; 8 in Fig 5), 'Input:/Output:' template, Foo/Bar targets in SUL-ICL, natural targets such as 'Negative Sentiment' in regular ICL; exemplars are listed in mixed class order, not grouped (App D); full prompt ends 'Input: <query>\nOutput:' and the model completes the label; no instruction text; flipped-label and SUL-ICL prompts are made by swapping the label strings

parameters.remapped_word_proportion: increasing percent of input words remapped (App B.2)
parameters.alternative_targets: numbers, letters, fruits, with reversals (App B.3)

other.eval_example_counts: 250 evaluation examples for Fig 13 (code-davinci-002); fewer where dataset smaller
other.access: OpenAI models via API; PaLM models internal
other.prompt_length: k=16 per class gives 32 exemplars per prompt; RTE with k=16 per class exceeds PaLM context length, so it is dropped for PaLM in Fig 16/17

metrics.name: accuracy
metrics.definition: share of evaluation examples classified correctly against unmodified ground-truth labels, averaged across datasets

baselines: polynomial SVM (scikit-learn svm.SVC(kernel='poly')) for linear classification
eval.protocol: Below 50% accuracy at 100% flipped labels means the model follows the exemplars over its prior. Single runs, no confidence intervals.

prompts.purpose: linear classification exemplar (16 integers; Foo negative, Bar positive)

evidence.quote: By default, we use k = 16 in-context exemplars per class

Prompts in a SUL-ICL and ﬂipped-label ICL setup can be
obtained by swapping labels with the desired labels

results.claim: text-davinci-002 falls from 90.3% accuracy with no flipped labels to 22.5% with all exemplar labels flipped, far below chance, so it follows the exemplars over its prior.
results.setup: Fig 2: average over the six binary tasks (SST-2, SUBJ, QQP, RTE, FP, ETHOS; TREC excluded as six-class), 100 evaluation examples per dataset, k=16 exemplars per class, evaluation labels not flipped.
results.quote: text-davinci-002 performance drops from 90.3% with 0% ﬂipped labels to just 22.5% with 100% ﬂipped labels

results.claim: Small models (all GPT-3 sizes, treated as small) stay near chance under flipped labels; they cannot override semantic priors.
results.setup: Fig 2, same setup as above; GPT-3 ada to davinci.
results.quote:
GPT-3 models can remove semantic
priors (i.e., perform at guessing accuracy) but cannot override them

results.claim: Standard PaLM reaches as low as 31% accuracy at 100% flipped labels, while Flan-PaLM does not get below chance.
results.setup: Fig 7: PaLM vs Flan-PaLM 8B/62B/540B, k=16 per class, 100 eval examples per dataset, averaged over six datasets.
results.note: Fig 7 caption says six datasets, but App C.1 says RTE is excluded for PaLM because k=16 prompts exceed context length, so PaLM averages may cover five datasets.
results.quote:
Standard PaLM models, on the other hand, could achieve as low as 31% accuracy when
presented with 100% ﬂipped labels

results.claim: Instruction tuning makes Flan-PaLM unable to override semantic priors beyond chance even at 100% flipped labels.
results.quote:
Flan-PaLM models were unable to override
their semantics more than what could be achieved by random guessing, even with 100% ﬂipped
labels

results.claim: Flan-PaLM-8B beats PaLM-8B in SUL-ICL by 9.6%, nearly matching PaLM-62B.
results.setup: Fig 6: SUL-ICL (Foo/Bar), PaLM vs Flan-PaLM, 2 to 16 exemplars per class, 100 eval examples per dataset, averaged over six datasets.
results.quote: Flan-PaLM-8B outperforms PaLM-8B by 9.6%, almost catching up to PaLM-62B

results.claim: Large models lose little when natural labels are replaced by semantically-unrelated labels; small models lose a lot.
results.setup: Fig 3: GPT-3, InstructGPT, Codex, PaLM; k=16 per class, 100 eval examples per dataset, average over datasets. The paper gives no number in text, only the figure. davinci behaves like a small model.
results.quote:
Large models, on the other hand, experience very small performance drops after this
change

results.claim: In SUL-ICL more exemplars help large models more than small ones.
results.setup: Fig 4: 2,4,8,16 exemplars per class; PaLM, Codex, ada/babbage/curie only; InstructGPT and davinci not run for cost.
results.quote: including more in-context exemplars results in a greater performance improvement for large models than it does for small models

results.claim: Some SUL-ICL tasks emerge only with scale: RTE near random for PaLM-8B and 62B but well above random for PaLM-540B; code-davinci-002 reaches 80%+ on RTE and ETHOS.
results.setup: Fig 5: k=8 exemplars per class, 100 eval examples, Codex and PaLM.

results.claim: The largest Codex model beats random on 16-dimensional linear classification by 19%, smaller ones by at most 9%.
results.setup: Fig 8: SUL-ICL Foo/Bar, N=16, k=16 per class, 100 eval examples, integer coordinates 1 to 1000.
results.quote:
the largest model outperforms random guessing by 19% on
this task, while smaller models cannot outperform random guessing by more than 9%

results.claim: code-davinci-002 can do linear classification up to N=64; smaller Codex reach guessing near N=16; all PaLM sizes work up to at least N=8; none beat an SVM baseline.
results.setup: Fig 21, k=16 per class, 100 eval examples.
results.quote: the largest model can successfully perform linear classiﬁcation up to N = 64

results.claim: Flipped-label ICL is harder than SUL-ICL; the gap reaches 74% for text-curie-001 on SST-2.
results.setup: Fig 10, k=16 per class, 100 eval examples; flipped-label accuracy computed by flipping evaluation labels.
results.quote:
performance differing by up to 74%
(text-curie-001 on SST-2)

results.claim: At 100% remapped input words even the largest models cannot beat random on almost all datasets.
results.setup: Fig 12, k=16 per class, 100 eval examples.
results.quote:
At 100% remapped input words, even the largest models (code-davinci-002 and
PaLM-540B) are unable to beat random guessing on almost all datasets

results.claim: Input format barely matters for SUL-ICL: mean accuracy across formats ranges 77.9% to 87.7%, within 6.3% of the 84.2% mean.
results.setup: Fig 14: code-davinci-002, k=16 per class, 100 eval examples, six alternative templates.
results.quote:
ranges from 77.9% to 87.7%) is within ±6.3% of the mean
(84.2%)

results.claim: Small InstructGPT models drop by up to 36% on out-of-distribution SST-2/Rotten Tomatoes SUL-ICL; text-curie-001 loses 4%, text-davinci-001 none.
results.setup: Table 2: InstructGPT a-1,b-1,c-1,d-1, SUL-ICL, k=16 per class, 100 eval examples.
results.note: Table 2 in-context SST-2 / eval RT: a-1 54, b-1 63, c-1 90, d-1 93 against baseline 80, 91, 94, 93.
results.quote: small models (e.g., text-ada-001 and text-babbage-001) suffer from signiﬁcant performance drops of up to 36%

limits: 100 evaluation examples per dataset; authors say they chose breadth over per-dataset precision and report no variance.
OpenAI and Codex model sizes are unknown and assumed to increase; InstructGPT vs GPT-3 cannot isolate instruction tuning.
davinci behaves like a small model and is unexplained.
Why scale unlocks these behaviours is left open.
Models are 2020-2022 vintage and tasks are classification only.
Linear classification does not improve with PaLM scale, so size alone is not the factor.

all labels in the exemplars are flipped while evaluation labels stay the same
